extracted.intended_audience: literate coffee-house readers and members of early 18th-century polite society (writers, critics, and patrons of the theatre)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards about literary style (especially panegyric), theatrical propriety, application of learning to public use, and accuracy of public signage aimed at contributors and readers in coffee-house periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity in pleasure (requirement of decency)
rubrics_metrics.description: “_res est severa voluptas_ — there is a certain severity in pleasure. Without that, all decency is banished; and if reason is not to be present at our greatest satisfactions, of all the races of creatures, the human is the most miserable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure ought to be tempered by a seriousness or restraint that preserves decency; reason must govern even our greatest satisfactions. Anti-pattern: unbridled pleasure without reason leads to indecency and misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit equals virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “When Virgil describes a wit, he always means a virtuous man; and all his sentiments of men of genius are such as show persons distinguished from the common level of mankind; such as placed happiness in the contempt of low fears, and mean gratifications."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being 'witty' is not merely cleverness of expression but a moral quality: genuine wit should be allied to virtue, wisdom, and contempt of petty fears and base gratifications. For writers and critics, praise of wit implies moral worth, not mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage morality and propriety
rubrics_metrics.description: On the puppet-show: it was remarked that 'it was against all morality, as well as rules of the stage, that Punch should be in jest in the Deluge, or indeed that he should appear at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic representation must observe moral appropriateness and unity of tone: comic or grotesque elements (e.g., Punch) are improper in scenes of high moral gravity (e.g., the Deluge). Anti-pattern: inserting incongruous humour into tragic or sacred scenes violates stage rules and audience decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panegyric by indirect praise (technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of panegyric 'consists in a certain artful way of conveying the applause in an indirect manner' — e.g., taking a man by surprise so that he receives you favourably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective praise is often indirect and unexpected: surprise the subject with praise so that antipathy turns to favour. Example anecdotes (Bacon/Tiberius) illustrate that sudden, artful commendation wins immediate goodwill. Anti-pattern: blunt, obvious flattery or ostentatious praise that the subject anticipates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panegyric style: elevated and obscure language to conceal flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of 'The Naked Truth': 'The language is extremely sublime, and not at all to be understood by the vulgar: the sentiments are such as would make no figure in ordinary words; but such is the art of the expression...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A style of lofty, obscure diction can disguise panegyric as serious discourse—appearing noble and profound while actually flattering. This is a technique of the courtier-writer: grand phrases and exalted metaphors mask the flattering intent. Anti-pattern: overly plain language that exposes the flattering purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply learning to useful public service
rubrics_metrics.description: “Men of wit do so much employ their thoughts upon fine speculations, that things useful to mankind are wholly neglected... It would be a happy thing, if such as have real capacities for public service, were employed in works of general use."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and men of letters should direct their abilities to practical matters of public utility rather than exclusively to abstruse or pedantic refinements. Recommendation to authorities: employ capable minds for collective benefit. Anti-pattern: wasting talent on trivial scholastic disputes while ignoring obvious civic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy in public inscriptions and orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint about 'so many gross errors... in the very directions of things, wherein accuracy is necessary for the conduct of life' and examples of misspelt sign-posts (e.g., 'This is the BEER' instead of 'This is the BEAR').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public signs and inscriptions must be correctly spelled and clearly depicted; bad spelling or poor painting misleads strangers and causes practical harm. This is an easily remediable social failing and should be corrected. Example illustrates real inconvenience caused by inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity in place-naming and distinguishing locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that 'Places are confounded, as well for want of proper distinctions... I found he mistook that for Charing Cross, by the erection of the like statue in each place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Municipal or private markers should avoid ambiguity—use clear distinguishing signs or inscriptions so that residents and visitors can reliably identify places. Anti-pattern: erecting indistinct or duplicate monuments/signs that cause confusion and misdirection.
